extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional comedy writers/screenwriters seeking or working in writing partnerships
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for choosing and working successfully with a comedy writing partner, covering selection, working methods, interpersonal dynamics, and dispute resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar sensibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you both have similar sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you love Patton Oswalt and his all-time favorite comedian is Pauley Shore, keep lookin'. (If his all-time favorite comedian is Pauley Shore keep looking even if your favorite funnyman is Dan Rather.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal chemistry / get-along factor
rubrics_metrics.description: You and your partner must genuinely get along personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There have been a number of sibling teams that have worked out. Make sure you and your sib really get along and your last name begins with C. (Humorous aside aside — emphasizes the importance of interpersonal compatibility.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary pairing (skill/configuration fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you complement each other then go for it; different configurations (e.g., male/female teams) can work if skills and sensibilities mesh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some of Hollywood’s most successful teams are mixed-gender partnerships. Example cited: Anne Flett Giordano & Chuck Ranberg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar work habits and environment preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you both have compatible work habits and preferred work environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you like to work in a quiet office during the day and she is only comfortable writing at the Viper Club after hours, continue your search. Align on where and when you write.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aligned aspirations and career goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Partners should have similar ambitions and end goals for their writing careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your goal is to be a writer and his is just to use this as a means to move into directing or to get chicks, pass. If he wants to write Oscar-winning movies in five years and you want to punch up Bette Midler’s Vegas act, don't partner up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreed working method / division of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide and agree in advance how you'll collaborate (e.g., head-to-head, split scenes, one drafts and the other rewrites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include: working head-to-head, splitting assignments and writing individual scenes, one person writing a rough draft and the other rewriting. Example of an unconventional method: one at the computer while the other floats on a raft—'What works for you?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching work tempo and deadline approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your approaches to starting, pacing, and meeting deadlines are compatible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Odd Couple would not make a good writing team: Felix would start right away and turn it in early; Oscar would wait until legal action was threatened. Both partners need to be of one temperament or the other (both proactive or both prone to delay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust and mutual respect
rubrics_metrics.description: You must trust and respect your partner's talent and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don’t think he’s the talented one of the two you haven’t found the right person. Respect doesn't mean always deferring—argument is normal—but the baseline must be mutual trust and respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep disagreements professional — don't make it personal
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue about script issues without letting disagreements bleed into personal feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DON'T MAKE IT PERSONAL. Think of TV wrestlers who 'kill each other on camera' and then go out for beers. Argue over script issues but don't let the disagreement affect the relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fight fair and use a practical decision rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Use fair, non-manipulative conflict behavior and a clear rule for resolving disputes about lines or jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No passive-aggressive behaviour, no mind games, no guilt trips. Policy example: both must agree before a line goes in; if you can’t agree and one can’t quickly convince the other, throw the line out and come up with something else — it's often faster to craft a new joke than spend hours arguing.
